beats.headline: REAL BAT BOMBS
beats.short_title: The US Really Built Bat Bombs 🦇 Meatball Investigates
beats.comment: Would you trust a bat with a bomb? 🦇 yes / 🙅 never
beats.caption: The US military really built bat bombs, and the bats set its own air base on fire.
beats.bonus: Project X-Ray: in 1942 dentist Lytle Adams pitched strapping tiny timed firebombs to Mexican free-tailed bats, and President Roosevelt approved it. On 15 May 1943 armed bats got loose and set the Carlsbad Army Airfield Auxiliary Air Base in New Mexico on fire. The program was cancelled in 1944 after about $2 million.
sources: Wikipedia, Bat bomb: proposed by dental surgeon Lytle S. Adams in January 1942; approved by President Roosevelt; Mexican free-tailed bats carrying small timed incendiaries were meant to roost in Japanese buildings; each bomb carrier held 1,040 bats; on 15 May 1943 armed bats were accidentally released, roosted under a fuel tank and set the Carlsbad Army Airfield Auxiliary Air Base test range on fire; the Navy took over in August 1943 (Project X-Ray); the chief chemist estimated 3,625-4,748 fires per load against 167-400 for regular incendiary bombs; Fleet Admiral Ernest King cancelled it in 1944 after about $2 million — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bat_bomb (checked 2026-11-02)

Carroll V. Glines, 'The Bat Bombers', Air & Space Forces Magazine (Air Force Association), 1 Oct 1990: about 3,500 bats collected at Carlsbad Caverns in May 1943; incendiaries of 17 g and 28 g, the larger burning six minutes; a handler left a door open and bats escaped with live incendiaries, setting fire to a hangar and a general's car (this account; the official report says only that a fire destroyed much of the test material); Roosevelt approved; an Army test burned a village simulating Japanese structures to the ground; about $2 million; cancelled by Adm. King — https://www.airandspaceforces.com/article/1090bat/ (checked 2026-11-02)
Wikimedia Commons, 'Carlsbad AAF Fire after Bat Bomb Accident.jpg' (USAAF, public domain): errant bats from the bat bomb set the Army Air Base in Carlsbad, New Mexico on fire
Jack Couffer, 'Bat Bomb: World War II's Other Secret Weapon' (University of Texas Press, 1992)

May 1943. They caught 3,500 bats at Carlsbad Caverns.

beats.say: One bomb could hold over a thousand bats.
Each one, a tiny firebomb that burns for six minutes.
But then, some armed bats got loose.

The Navy cancelled it anyway, after two million dollars.
Final score: bats, one. US Army, zero.
